course:
This course has broadened my understanding of how literature interacts with historical events, especially during moments of political instability and cultural transformation. Exploring texts from the Civil War and Restoration period allowed me to see how writers responded to censorship, upheaval, and changing moral codes in clever, satirical, and often subversive ways.

One of the things I appreciated most was how much I learned without even realizing it. Through writing my commonplace book, I was able to make sense of unfamiliar ideas, track patterns across different texts, and reflect on themes that still feel relevant today. Even though I didn’t study by memorizing definitions, I feel like many of the key concepts have become second nature.

course:
"Civil War and Restoration" period only cover up to 20-30 years which means in this course, you will also deal with seventeenth century and various works from eighteenth century. Be prepared -If you love this major, no problem. The overall structure of the course is smooth, and the literary works we study are analyzed in a meaningful and engaging way, which I feel like learning somethings.
Participation counts for 30% of the final grade, which may seem high at first. However, as long as you attend regularly, arrive on time, stay engaged (i.e., avoid sleeping or using their phones excessively), contribute occasionally in discussions, and complete the assignments, earning a good participation grade is very achievable. 
The only slightly overwhelming part of the course is the final project—the commonplace book. While it's a creative and unique assignment, it can become demanding at times, especially when searching for content, writing by hand, and adding visual elements like drawings or stickers. Still, I would say that Ivana was so understanding in many times, so do your best and enjoy. I did enjoy!

the commonplace book assignment seems like a lot at first, but is usually fun when you get into it because you can prepare the pages about anything as long as the content is related to the course. I like that we are guided by interest in this project, and there are no strict limitations. also, the project makes a lot of sense in my opinion since we generally don't have enough time to cover all the aspects of a topic in class, so we get to learn more about that topic by researching about it outside of class.
other than that, the participation grade is unusually high, but the good part is that you can gain points for it not by just talking in class, but also by doing the required work, and showing the instructor that you did the work.
I also like that there is no final exam, since exams suck, especially if you have anxiety like I do. however, there was a midterm exam, and it consisted of simple, short answer questions, which seems great at first, until you realize that there is not much you can do if you don't have that clear, to the point short answer the instructor is looking for. so, there was not much room for commentary or analysis on the midterm, which is a minus aspect regarding that exam if you ask me. also, sometimes the instructor told us that she's giving away the questions she's going to ask on the exam, and then she didn't ask them even though she said she would, which is a bit annoying. she also said dates regarding events or people in general were not important, since we would forget them in a short time anyway, but then asked about them on the exam, which made her seem a bit unpredictable in that regard. but overall, I generally like her and this course.

Bir mail yazmayı bile çok görüyor (sorumuzun cevabı pdf’te veya bize atılan maillerde geçmiyordu, supervisorlarımız da bize koordinatör ile konuşmamız gerektiğini iletti—öbür türlü zaten biz de Ivana’yla muhattap olmaya bayılmıyoruz).
 
Öğrencilerle bitirme projesi süreci hakkında konuşmayacaksan koordinatör olma o zaman? Hoca hiç olma. Acilen 490 koordinatörünün değişmesi lazım. Rezil biri—umarım en tez vakitte kendine “layık” gördüğü bir üniversiteye geçer de bizi sürekli aşağılamasından kurtuluruz.
Ne öğretmeyi ne de not vermeyi biliyor. Öğrencileriyle iletişimi çok kötü. Hiçbir ödevde ne istediğini tam anlatmıyor ve çok saçma bir notlandırma kriteryası var.

I know this is so that we can learn as much as possible, but at times I felt a bit lost in her lectures, not being sure of where to direct my attention to amongst everything that was being mentioned. That being said, she teaches very well, what she expects from her students is very clear, and her capability to initiate class discussions made this course so fun!

When I compare it with the other ELIT professor that we took a class from in the first grade, Ivana Hoca's expectations are pretty unique and, I think, unnecessary. She wants us to come up with a completely different idea, which is hard because the books were literally written ages ago and give a grade lower than the bare minimum. For the presentations, she just graded them; she did not provide feedback, which is problematic since we do not know where we lost the points. Her classes are usually fun, but sometimes she is intense. I am happy she came to our department, but I hope her grading scheme will change and she will be more open about the essays.

Dr Bičak’s best quality is her willingness to hear students out if they can’t make it to class due to any illness. She more than makes up for this by otherwise treating students in a manner that is demeaning, belittling, and, occasionally, racist. Dr Bičak shows blatant favouritism towards a particular group of students. There is a clear divide between her in-group, and the rest of us who, to her mind, lack enthusiasm—meaning we have not fallen over ourselves to sing her praises. Although a huge portion of our grade depends on participation, class discussions are dominated by her handful of favourites, while the rest of us, try as we might, are barely allowed room to speak. In the few occasions that she does grace us with the opportunity to make a comment, she is quick to cut us off or speak over us. However, I must admit that there is a line she will not cross in her favouritism: Dr Bičak expects that all her students, equally, are stupid. Although this is a third-year elective class, she operates on the continuous assumption that we have been taught nothing in our previous classes and treats us as such. She often speaks—or, rather, rants—about how she “cannot teach us everything” just because our other instructors have failed to do so. On a good day, she is merely presumptuous. On a bad one, she is downright condescending. Dr Bičak is in the habit of “correcting” students’ pronunciations, calling them out in front of the whole class. More often than not, this has very little to do with mispronunciation and quite a bit to do with the fact that most of us, given that English is by no means our first language, have an accent. Dr Bičak wholly disregards this fact and will interrupt students, over and over, until she is satisfied with their pronunciation.

She is an excellent teacher, taking this elective course from her has been one of the highlights of my semester. I have learned a lot from her. I personally think this course should be mandatory for our department since it builds crucial basis for our further education.

Professor Bicak is an effective and knowledgeable instructor. I like the way she teaches the course by going over the texts with the class, and her slides are usually very helpful for me as a visual learner. For the most part, I liked the texts she chose for this course. I also appreciated that she helped us form connections between subjects and wanted to make sure that we learned the subject completely. However, she expects proper discipline from students and wants you to put genuine effort into the course. She's also highly against disruptive behavior, so if you struggle with any of these things, you might face difficulties in her class. She also has a tendency to tune out anything outside the class environment, which affects the class both positively and negatively.

She is an intelligent person, and I don't agree with any bad comments about her in the evaluations since, as far as you have done what she asks for, there is no chance you will pass this course with a low grade. The things that she asks for are for you to improve yourself in the course content, and in this process, she has been doing everything to help you. The topics she covers are pretty fun and interesting. I recommend that you select her classes if you really want to learn something.
course: The strongest aspect of this course, for me, was its content, as someone highly interested in Greek and Roman mythology. Although I'm not particularly interested in the religious part, both parts are equally important for understanding their impact on English literature. Even though I was already familiar with the Classical topics, going over them wasn't boring at all. For the Religious part, I learned a lot about Christianity and how it shaped today's literature. I think this course includes subjects that all ELIT students should know of. If anyone's considering taking this elective, I highly recommend it. However, I advise you to make sure you update your Commonplace Book regularly, which is considered the final for this course, as it counts for half of your grade and it is very hard to get back on track if you start neglecting it during the term.

Taking this course has been a valuable experience that deepened my understanding of the foundations of English literature. One of the most rewarding aspects was working on the commonplace book. It pushed me to actively engage with the texts and reflect critically on the themes and ideas we discussed in class. Through this process, I learned a great deal—not just about content, but also about how to think more analytically.

I also gained a solid grasp of many key terms and concepts. While I didn’t approach the course by rote memorization, the ideas have stuck with me in a more intuitive way—it often feels like the knowledge is right at my fingertips when I need it. This kind of familiarity has made it easier to participate in discussions and write about complex material with more confidence.

Most importantly, the course has helped me develop my critical analysis skills. I’ve become more attentive to how classical and religious narratives continue to shape literary traditions and cultural assumptions. Overall, this course has given me not only knowledge but also sharper tools to approach literature with greater depth.

I found the course comprehensive and got a lot out of it. We moved through the Bible section quickly, but still, I learned a lot about the topic. The commonplace book was a lot of work, but it allowed us to dive deeper into topics we were genuinely interested in, which made it worthwhile. Also, keeping a commonplace book deepened my understanding of the material. This course should be a mandatory class in the first year rather than just an elective.

The first issue this course runs into is the grading breakdown: 20% - midterm, 30% - participation, 50% - final project. At face value, this may seem strange and perhaps a little extreme. Having made the mistake of going through with this course, I can confirm that this was an utter nightmare. To start with, this is an ELIT class offered by an ELIT instructor that has not a single essay requirement. Instead, our only real assignment was a fill-in-the-blank exam that required no critical thinking. The participation requirement is no less ridiculous; in Dr Bičak’s own words, “participation isn’t just about being active in class,” which I believe gives a sufficient idea of the sheer absurdity that surrounded most of her expectations. “Participation,” in this course, meant annotating our course packs and having them checked by Dr Bičak in a manner that was oddly reminiscent of the fifth grade. However, it was the final project that was easily the worst part of this course: the commonplace book. This is not to say that I take issue with keeping a commonplace book. The issue lies in the fact that Dr Bičak seems to fundamentally misunderstand what a commonplace book is. By virtue of it being a commonplace book, it is frankly absurd to grade it in any capacity. A commonplace book is a rough collection of one’s thoughts and ideas. This cannot feasibly be transformed into a project worth 50% of the overall grade. What Dr Bičak is actually interested in is a journal—one that may be better suited to Pinterest than a university-level course and the grading policies of which seemed to have been established upon a whim that can be swayed this way or that. There is not a single clear expectation provided, and any attempt to provide one has been in the form of meaningless, empty words that offer absolutely no clarity. While the premise of this course—in its topic and its readings—was very interesting, it is the actual execution of it that has completely failed.

Since it's an elective class, it's up to the student to know themselves and how much they really want to take it. Personally, the course was beyond enjoyable and we did so many different things in the syllabus as well as some fun and different activities in class. I think the course really cultivated my love for Greek and Roman history, culture, and mythology. And it was very interesting to learn about the different parts of the Bible, such as Old Testament, new Testament, Psalms, Gospels etc. I would definitely reccomend this course for those who are willing to learn in class as well as put in the work on their own learning through tasks such as the commonplace book, where we have great creative freedom and can research the things we're interested in.
